title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Iterative radix-2 divider, merged 33x33 multiplier, and redirect decoupled from load-use detect
motivation:
Baseline Fmax is 5.44 MHz: the worst path (199.8 ns, 150 logic levels) is
MEM/WB.rd -> forward_unit -> EX forward mux -> alu.sv -> dmem BSRAM address
register. The 150 levels are the fully combinational 32-bit `/` and `%` in
alu.sv. CoreMark's timed loop executes almost no DIV/REM, so this logic buys
~0 IPC while it divides Fmax by ~10x.

Measured during hypothesis generation (Gowin flow, place option 0, same
tools/eval/gowin.py build on a scratch copy of rtl/):
  - div/rem removed, three multipliers merged into one 33x33: 49.41 MHz,
    20 levels, 1971 LUT (vs 12312), 2 DSP (vs 6).
  - div/rem AND all multipliers removed: 46.73 MHz (i.e. the single-cycle
    DSP multiplier is NOT on the critical path; keep MUL single-cycle).
The new worst path (~25.5 ns) is: regfile LUT-RAM DO (sync-read, ID/EX
rs*_val flop absorbed) -> write-first bypass mux -> EX forward mux ->
32-bit branch compare carry chain -> redirect -> if_stage NOP mux
(out.instr = redirect ? NOP : imem_data) -> hazard_unit load-use rs1/rs2
compare -> stall/flush_id -> ID/EX register RESET. The if_stage-NOP ->
hazard compare leg (~4 LUT levels + routing) is logically redundant.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three localized micro-optimizations:

(A) Sequential divider. Replace combinational DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU with a
radix-2 restoring divider (1 quotient bit/cycle, ~33-34 cycles) that stalls
the front of the pipeline while a divide sits in EX. Expected: Fmax
5.4 -> ~49 MHz (measured), IPC loss << 1%.

(B) Merge the three 64-bit products (mul_ss, mul_uu, mul_su) into ONE
`$signed({a_ext,a}) * $signed({b_ext,b})` with a_ext = a[31] & (MULH|MULHSU),
b_ext = b[31] & MULH; MUL = prod[31:0], MULH/MULHU/MULHSU = prod[63:32].
Single-cycle; saves 4 DSP and the wide product mux (area/routing relief).

(C) Take `redirect` off the hazard/ID path. load_use_hazard requires
ID/EX.ctrl.mem_read = 1, while redirect requires ID/EX to hold a
branch/jump, so they are mutually exclusive — but synthesis cannot prove
it, so today redirect -> NOP mux -> rs1/rs2 compare -> flush_id is timed.
Change: hazard_unit compares against the RAW imem instruction bits
(io_imemData[19:15] / [24:20], not the NOP-substituted if_id_w.instr).
Optionally also qualify load_use with !redirect is NOT needed (exclusive).
In if_stage the NOP/valid mux may keep `redirect`, because on redirect ID/EX
is either flushed (flush_id) or held (dmem_stall) and never captures IF's
output — the implementer may drop redirect from that mux as well to shorten
redirect -> decoder -> ID/EX data paths, but ID/EX flush on redirect MUST stay.
Expected: ~5-10% more Fmax on top of (A).

Net: fitness ≈ 49-54 MHz × ~2.22 iter/MHz ≈ 110-120 iter/s vs 12.12
(≈ +800%; field below is schema-capped at +50).

Implementation details for (A):
1. New rtl/divider.sv, start/busy/done handshake. On start latch operands,
   is_signed, is_rem; take absolute values for signed ops; 32 shift-subtract
   iterations (33-bit subtract); sign fix-up (quotient negated iff operand
   signs differ, remainder takes dividend sign). Explicitly override RV32M
   special cases: b==0 -> q=0xFFFFFFFF, r=a; a==INT_MIN && b==-1 (signed)
   -> q=INT_MIN, r=0. Result held until consumed. Optional cheap early-out:
   b==0 completes immediately.
2. ex_stage.sv: is_div = in.valid && alu_op in {DIV,DIVU,REM,REMU}. Start the
   divider on the FIRST cycle the op is in EX and latch the forwarded rs1/rs2
   then (later forwarding can be stale because older instructions retire
   while EX is busy). div_stall = is_div && !div_done. While div_stall and
   !stall_ex_mem: EX/MEM captures a BUBBLE (valid=0 and ctrl='0 so
   reg_write/mem_read/mem_write/is_jump are 0 — mem_stage and forward_unit do
   not look at valid). When done, EX/MEM captures the divider result as
   alu_result and the LATCHED operands as rs1_val/rs2_val (RVFI). The
   divider returns to idle only on the cycle EX/MEM actually accepts (not
   during a dmem stall). Back-to-back divides must each restart.
3. hazard_unit.sv: new input div_stall; stall_if |= div_stall;
   stall_id |= div_stall; flush_id must not fire from load_use while
   div_stall (hold, not bubble) — mirror existing dmem_stall priority.
   A divide never redirects, so no redirect/div conflict.
4. alu.sv: delete real `/` and `%` (ALU output for div ops is ignored).
5. ALTOPS (formal): checks run at depth 20; a 33-cycle divider would starve
   liveness/insn. Under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS keep the SAME
   start/busy/done handshake but complete after 1 cycle with the ALTOPS
   formula ((a-b)^const) on the latched operands, so the stall/latch/bubble
   machinery stays inside the formal proof. ALTOPS MUL* formulas stay in alu.
6. Tests: DIV/REM vectors (incl. div-by-zero, INT_MIN/-1, sign mixes) move to
   a new test/test_divider.py that drives start and waits for done; MUL*
   vectors stay in test/test_alu.py. Cosim covers the pipeline stall path.

title: Multi-cycle iterative divider off the EX path + decouple redirect from hazard/decode
motivation:
Fmax is 5.44 MHz. The worst path (199.8 ns, 156 cells) is
clock -> u_fwd -> u_ex -> u_alu -> EX/MEM: a fully combinational 32-bit
`/` and `%` (four restoring-divide arrays) sits inside the single-cycle
ALU behind the forwarding mux. MEASURED during hypothesis generation: a
throwaway run with `make timing TARGET=bench` and only the DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU
arms stubbed out reached **46.5 MHz** (21 logic levels, 2110 logic cells,
6 DSP). That is 8.5x the current Fmax, and the multiplier was still fully
combinational in EX. So the divider alone sets the clock period for every
instruction, while the timed CoreMark region almost never divides (-O3
lowers constant divides to MULH; list/matrix/state/crc have almost no
runtime `/`/`%`). With the divider gone, the new worst path (26.8 ns) was
regfile/ID/EX regs -> u_ex (fwd + branch compare -> redirect) -> u_if
(NOP-substitute mux on IF/ID instr) -> u_hazard (load-use rs compare) ->
ID/EX reset/CE and PC CE. That chain is logically redundant (see 2).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
1. Iterative divider (main change). Remove `/` and `%` from alu.sv. Add
   `rtl/divider.sv`, a radix-2 restoring/non-restoring divider that
   produces one quotient bit per cycle (~33 cycles). It works on unsigned
   magnitudes and fixes signs at the end. RV32M corner cases are explicit:
   div-by-zero gives q=all-ones, r=dividend; INT_MIN/-1 gives q=INT_MIN,
   r=0. Handshake in EX:
   - When a valid DIV-class op is in ID/EX and the unit is idle, latch the
     *post-forward* rs1/rs2 in that first cycle. Forwarding sources drain
     away while EX waits, so they must be captured then.
   - While busy, assert `ex_busy`. The hazard unit turns that into
     stall_if and stall_id (hold PC and ID/EX, no flush). EX/MEM captures
     a bubble (valid=0, reg_write=0, no mem op).
   - On done, EX/MEM captures the quotient or remainder plus the latched
     rs1/rs2 (for RVFI rs*_rdata), and the unit goes idle. It must not
     restart on the same ID/EX entry: use a done/"result consumed" flag.
   - If EX/MEM is held by dmem_stall when the result is ready, keep it
     until EX/MEM advances.
   - A divide in EX never redirects, so flushes cannot hit it.
   Under `RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` the same handshake finishes in 1 cycle and
   returns the ALTOPS formulas ((a-b)^const). That keeps the 20-step BMC
   tractable while still testing stall/bubble/operand-latch/order logic.

2. Decouple redirect from the hazard/decode input (secondary change;
   targets the measured next-worst path). Today if_stage forces
   IF/ID.instr to NOP when `flush || redirect`, and hazard_unit compares
   that muxed instr's rs1/rs2 with ID/EX.rd. When redirect=1, ID/EX holds
   the branch or jump that caused it, so id_ex.mem_read=0 and load-use is
   already 0. flush_id=redirect also clears ID/EX, and redirect already
   has priority over stall at the PC. So the redirect term in the IF/ID
   NOP mux changes nothing. Fix:
   - Drive hazard_unit's if_id_rs1/rs2 from raw `io_imemData[19:15]` /
     `[24:20]`.
   - Drop `redirect` from if_stage's instr/valid mux (keep the imem_stall
     term, which does produce a real bubble).
   - Leave the ID/EX capture with the existing flush_id priority.
   This takes the branch-compare -> redirect chain out of the decode and
   load-use logic cones, leaving only redirect -> PC mux and
   redirect -> ID/EX clear.

3. Multiplier: keep it single-cycle in EX (it is not on the measured
   critical path). Merge the three 64-bit products into one 33x33 signed
   multiply with op-dependent operand extension (MUL/MULHU zero-extended,
   MULH sign-extended, MULHSU a signed / b unsigned). This saves DSPs and
   LUTs and shortens the ALU output mux. Keep the ALTOPS and real branches
   consistent.

Expected: Fmax >= 46 MHz (measured with change 1 alone), likely 50-60 MHz
with change 2. CPI cost is about 33 cycles per rare runtime divide. Net
fitness is roughly 8x the baseline (12 -> ~90-110 iter/s), far above the
+50% schema cap. LUT count should also fall a lot (the stubbed run
used 2110 logic cells vs 12312 LUT4 at baseline).

title: IF-stage BTB + 2-bit bimodal + 4-entry RAS, EX-verified next-PC prediction
motivation:
The core has no prediction at all: next_pc is always pc+4, and every taken
branch, JAL and JALR redirects from EX. Because IF and ID are merged (the
IF payload feeds the ID/EX register combinationally), each taken
control-flow instruction costs one bubble: the wrong-path pc+4 fetch is
killed and ID/EX gets a bubble. CoreMark -O3 on RV32IM has about 18%
conditional branches (roughly 55-60% taken) plus 3-4% JAL/JALR, so about
13% of dynamic instructions are taken control flow. That is about 0.13 CPI
on a measured CPI of about 1.5 (2.23 iter/Mcycle), or roughly 8-9% of all
cycles. Fmax is 5.44 MHz, set by the 199 ns combinational divider path
(fwd -> ex -> alu). A small IF-side predictor is nowhere near that path,
so any IPC gain shows up almost 1:1 in fitness. The hot CoreMark loops
(matrix loops, list traversal, crc loops, state-machine loops) are
dominated by backward loop branches and unconditional jumps. A bimodal
BTB predicts these well.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a next-PC predictor in IF that the EX stage verifies. A correctly
predicted taken branch or jump then costs 0 bubbles instead of 1.
Mispredicts cost 1 bubble, which is the same as today's cost for every
taken branch. No case gets slower than the baseline.

1. New module rtl/branch_predictor.sv:
   - 64-entry direct-mapped BTB indexed by pc[7:2]. Each entry holds
     tag = pc[15:8], target[31:2], a 2-bit saturating counter and a
     2-bit type (00 = cond branch, 01 = plain jump JAL/JALR,
     10 = call: JAL/JALR with rd in {x1,x5},
     11 = return: JALR with rd = x0 and rs1 in {x1,x5}).
   - Store tag, target, ctr and type in arrays with no reset, so Gowin
     can infer async-read LUT-RAM (one write port, driven from EX).
     Keep the 64 valid bits in a separate flop vector that is cleared
     on reset.
   - Combinational lookup on the current IF pc:
     hit = valid[idx] && tag match.
     pred_taken = hit && (type == cond ? ctr[1] : 1).
     pred_target = (type == ret && ras_count != 0) ? ras_top
                                                   : {target, 2'b00}.
   - 4-entry return address stack (circular pointer plus saturating
     count). It is updated only at EX, not speculatively. EX pushes
     pc+4 for a call and pops for a return, and only when the EX/MEM
     register actually advances (!stall_ex_mem && in.valid &&
     !misalign_fault). The dmem-stall cycles that re-evaluate the same
     EX instruction must not push or pop twice. Mispredicts caused by a
     stale RAS are always caught by EX, so they only cost performance.
   - BTB update at EX, gated the same way, for every valid branch or
     jump without a misalign fault. Carry the IF-time hit bit and ctr
     value down the pipe and compute the new counter from the carried
     value, so the update is a single write with no read-modify-write
     at EX:
       - Taken conditional branch: allocate or refresh the entry with
         ctr = hit ? sat_inc(ctr) : 2'b10 and the target.
       - Not-taken conditional branch: update only if it hit
         (ctr = sat_dec). Do not allocate on a miss.
       - JAL/JALR: write the entry with ctr = 2'b11, the appropriate
         type and the actual target.
       - Optional: if a valid non-control-flow instruction was
         predicted taken (tag alias), clear that entry's valid bit.

2. rtl/if_stage.sv:
   next_pc = redirect ? redirect_target
           : pred_taken ? pred_target : pc + 4.
   Redirect keeps priority over stall, and stall still holds the PC.
   Add pred_taken, pred_target, pred_hit and pred_ctr to if_id_t. They
   must be forced to 0 whenever the IF payload is invalid (flush,
   redirect or imem stall).

3. rtl/core_pkg.sv and rtl/id_stage.sv:
   Add the same prediction fields to if_id_t and id_ex_t, and pass them
   through the ID/EX register. The existing flush that zeroes the whole
   register also clears them.

4. rtl/ex_stage.sv:
   - Compute actual_next with the same expression that already feeds
     pc_next: pc+4 on misalign fault, jump_target for jumps,
     branch_target when a branch is taken, otherwise pc+4.
   - pred_next = in.pred_taken ? in.pred_target : in.pc + 4.
   - redirect = in.valid && (actual_next != pred_next).
   - redirect_target = actual_next. The redirect target is now pc+4
     when a branch was predicted taken but is not taken.
   - Leave RVFI pc_wdata / pc_next unchanged. It is still the
     architectural next PC.
   - Export the update/RAS signals: valid-advance strobe, is_branch,
     is_jump, is_call, is_ret, taken, target, carried hit and ctr.
   - Optional timing hygiene for later rounds: for branches and JAL the
     target is pc+imm, which does not depend on forwarding. Compute
     "pred_target == pc+imm" in ID and register it as one bit, so that
     only JALR needs a 32-bit compare after the forwarding muxes.

5. rtl/core.sv:
   Instantiate branch_predictor. Wire the IF-side lookup (pc in,
   prediction out) and the EX-side update, gated by !stall_ex_mem.
   hazard_unit stays unchanged: its `redirect` input now means
   "mispredict".

Correctness is independent of predictor state, because every retired
instruction's successor is checked against the architectural next PC
in EX. Uninitialised or aliased BTB/RAS contents, and arbitrary
symbolic instruction streams in riscv-formal, can only cost cycles.
Liveness is unaffected, since each EX instruction still advances.

Expected gain: the BTB should catch about 85-90% of taken conditional
branches in the CoreMark hot loops and nearly all JALs, and the RAS
covers crcu8/crcu16-style multi-call-site returns. That removes about
0.10-0.11 of the 0.13 CPI of taken-control-flow bubbles, about 7-8% IPC.
Fmax should stay flat because the divider path is untouched and the
predictor's pc -> LUT-RAM -> tag compare -> next_pc path is about 15 ns
against the 199 ns critical path. The design adds about 300-600 LUT4
and about 80 FFs.

changes.description: New module: 64-entry direct-mapped BTB (tag pc[15:8], target[31:2], 2-bit ctr, 2-bit type) in async-read LUT-RAM plus a reset valid-bit vector, and a 4-entry return address stack. Combinational IF-side lookup; single EX-side write port, with RAS push/pop gated on the EX/MEM advance strobe.
Add pred_taken, pred_target[31:0], pred_hit and pred_ctr[1:0] to if_id_t and id_ex_t.

Take prediction inputs from branch_predictor. next_pc = redirect ? redirect_target : (pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4). Redirect keeps priority over stall. Drive the prediction fields in the IF payload, zeroed when flush, redirect or imem stall makes the payload invalid.

title: Flop regfile + dedicated AGU + multiplier product registered at EX/MEM (MUL-use interlock)
motivation:
Measured with `make timing TARGET=bench` (place option 0) during
hypothesis generation.

are tied (25.228 / 25.221 ns) and share a ~5 ns prefix: the register file

io_dmemAddr = EX/MEM.alu_result is absorbed into the dmem address

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three Fmax-only micro-opts. The first two are measured, and the third
targets the measured next wall.

1. Register-file as flops. Put (* syn_ramstyle = "registers" *) on
   reg_file.regs; keep the reset, x0 and write-first bypass semantics.
   ID/EX rs1_val/rs2_val become real flops (tC2Q 0.23 ns instead of the
   2.26 ns BSRAM plus bypass LUT).
2. Dedicated AGU. In EX, register reg_q.mem_addr <= rs1 (post-forward)
   + in.imm into a new ex_mem_t.mem_addr field. mem_stage uses in.mem_addr
   for dmem_addr, byte_mask, misalign check, load-extract shift and RVFI
   aligned_addr. alu_result stays for forwarding and WB.
3. Multiplier split across EX/MEM. The ALU no longer muxes the product
   into alu_result. EX computes the 33x33 signed product (same a_ext /
   b_ext scheme, with the ext bits decoded from the registered alu_op)
   and registers the needed 32-bit half (prod[31:0] for MUL, prod[63:32]
   for MULH/MULHSU/MULHU) into a new ex_mem_t.mul_res field. The field is
   written directly from the DSP output, with only a 2:1 low/high select
   that can come from a registered bit, and no ALU result mux. It also
   gets an is_mul ctrl bit. mem_stage writes
   MEM/WB.alu_result = is_mul ? mul_res : alu_result, so WB, RVFI rd_wdata
   and MEM/WB->EX forwarding see the product. EX/MEM->EX forwarding of a
   MUL is never used: hazard_unit treats a MUL in ID/EX exactly like a
   load (the load-use condition becomes
   (id_ex_mem_read || id_ex_is_mul) && rd matches), so a dependent
   instruction directly behind a MUL gets one bubble and then takes the
   MEM/WB forward. The ALTOPS stand-ins for MUL* must move to the same
   mul_res register path (the result for rd_wdata still equals the
   ALTOPS formula), so formal still covers the new interlock and
   forwarding.

6 ns). The critical path becomes forward -> branch compare -> redirect
-> PC (~17.4 ns) or forward -> adder/shifter -> alu_result, giving about

consumer is the very next instruction stalls one cycle; CoreMark
matrix_mul has few such back-to-back pairs at -O3, so the cost should
be about 1-2% of cycles.

title: Split EX: dedicated AGU drives dmem, MUL pipelined into MEM (load-like interlock), valid-only redirect flush, registered one-hot bypass selects
motivation:
I ran `make timing TARGET=bench` on the 53.4 MHz champion. Two path families
tie at about 25.2 ns (data delay 19.9 ns at the 5 ns constraint, so ~50 MHz on
this seed):
 (1) regfile BSRAM DO (tC2Q 2.26 ns) -> write-first bypass LUT
     (u_id rs2_val_s14) -> 3 LUT levels of forwarding mux
     (u_ex rs2_s9/s8/s7) -> alu_b mux -> **DSP multiplier** (3.78 ns,
     prod_65_s1) -> 5 LUT levels of ALU-result / dmem_addr mux
     (dmem_addr_c_*_s17/s9/s4/s1/s0) -> dmem BSRAM ADB. The testbench dmem is
     async-read, so Gowin absorbs EX/MEM.alu_result into the BSRAM
     read-address register. The whole ALU, including the multiplier and its
     19-way result mux, therefore sits in front of BSRAM address setup, even
     though a load or store address is only rs1+imm and the BSRAM uses only
     bits [12:2].
 (2) regfile BSRAM -> bypass LUT -> 3 forwarding-mux levels -> 3.1 ns route
     -> branch-compare carry chain -> 4 LUT levels of taken / misalign /
     redirect (u_if n328_*) -> flush_id (u_id n91) -> a fanout-33 buffer tree
     -> the synchronous RESET pin of every ID/EX data flop (rs1_val, rs2_val,
     ...). Flushing a wrong-path instruction only needs its valid and control
     bits cleared, but today redirect resets hundreds of data bits.
Paths 1-25 of the report are all one of these two families. No IPC-side
change can pay for this: every EX-stage path runs about 5 LUT levels plus a
DSP too long.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure the EX stage so that no single-cycle path contains more than one
"big" element (carry chain OR DSP OR BSRAM setup). Software-visible pipeline
timing is unchanged except for a one-cycle MUL-use interlock.

A. Dedicated AGU -> dmem. In EX, compute agu = fwd_rs1 + imm with its own
   adder, reading the forwarded rs1 directly and not the alu_a/alu_b muxes.
   Register it into a new EX/MEM.mem_addr, which alone drives io_dmemAddr,
   the byte mask, misalign detection, the load shift and RVFI mem_addr.
   BSRAM-address path: bypass -> fwd -> 13-bit carry chain -> ADB (about 10
   ns instead of 19.9). Loads write back load data and stores write nothing,
   so alu_result is never consumed for memory ops.

B. MUL pipelined across EX->MEM, interlocked like a load. Take the multiplier
   out of the ALU result mux. The 33x33 DSP product (operands straight from
   the forwarded rs1/rs2, sign-extension bits from alu_op) is registered at
   the EX/MEM boundary. Either register the whole 64-bit product and choose
   hi/lo in MEM, or register only the needed half using a hi/lo bit decoded
   in ID. Gowin can then put the product register into the DSP output
   register. In MEM, the MUL result joins the load-data mux that produces the
   MEM/WB write-back value. hazard_unit's load-use check becomes
   (id_ex.mem_read | id_ex.is_mul) against the next instruction's rs1/rs2,
   with the same one-bubble / dmem-stall-precedence rules. Consumers then
   always get the product from MEM/WB, just like load data. Cost: CoreMark
   -O3 issues roughly 3k MULs per iteration (mostly matrix_mul_*; N ~ 11 for
   the 2K set) against about 449k cycles, so at most ~0.7% extra cycles even
   if every MUL is immediately consumed. The ALTOPS stand-ins
   ((a+b)^const etc.) must go through exactly the same EX-register / MEM-select
   path so formal still proves the interlock and bypass.

C. Single write-back value in MEM/WB. In MEM, compute result =
   mem_to_reg ? load_data : (is_mul ? mul_sel : alu_result) before the MEM/WB
   register; the MEM path runs from BSRAM tC2Q through the load shift, about
   6-7 ns, so it has slack. fwd_mem_wb and the regfile write data then come
   straight from flops, which removes a LUT level from every EX-operand path.

D. Registered one-hot forwarding selects. Compute the forwarding decision one
   cycle early, in ID, for the instruction that will occupy ID/EX next cycle
   (the incoming instruction, or the held one on stall_id). Compare it against
   the rd/reg_write that will occupy EX/MEM and MEM/WB next cycle. Those
   "next-cycle occupants" are small control muxes of the current
   ID/EX/EX/MEM/MEM/WB rd fields, selected by stall_ex_mem / div_stall /
   hold_mem_wb, and they respect x0 and the EX/MEM > MEM/WB priority. Register
   the result as one-hot selects in ID/EX. The EX operand mux becomes a flat
   AND-OR with early, registered selects: 1-2 LUT levels instead of the
   current 3 plus compare logic. Preferred: also fold the regfile's
   write-first bypass in as a 4th one-hot source (wb_q = last cycle's regfile
   write data, captured when the write address matched), which removes the
   post-BSRAM bypass LUT. The held-operand case must stay correct: when ID/EX
   holds for several cycles, refresh rs*_val from the forwarded operand, or
   keep the select pointing at a stable source. Formal checks plus the
   dmem/imem-stall cosim will catch mistakes here.

E. Valid-only redirect/load-use flush, and branch misalignment known in ID.
   On flush_id, clear only ID/EX.valid and the ctrl bits that have side
   effects (reg_write, mem_read, mem_write, is_branch, is_jump, is_mul, the
   divide op / is_div). Leave the 32-bit data fields (pc, rs*_val, imm,
   instr, rd, rs*_addr) unreset, so redirect drives about 15 flops instead of
   hundreds of RESET pins. Because PC[1:0] is always 00 (no C extension), a
   taken-branch or JAL misalignment is just imm[1]. Decode it in ID and carry
   it in ctrl. Only JALR needs the post-forward jalr_sum[1]. The
   redirect/taken logic then drops about 2 LUT levels (misalign no longer
   waits on branch_target[1:0]). RVFI behaviour on trap is unchanged:
   is_illegal=1, reg_write=0, and pc_next = pc+4 on misaligned targets.

Expected result: path (1) drops to about 10-12 ns and path (2) to about
13-14 ns. The next limits should be the shifter/ALU -> EX/MEM path
(bypass + fwd + 3-4 shifter levels + a 2-level result mux, ~14 ns) and the
dmem_ready -> stall CE fanout. Fmax should land around 63-70 MHz (median seed)
against 53.4 MHz, at <1% more cycles, for a net gain of about +18-28% in
CoreMark iter/s.

title: Fetch-time decode-target prediction: 256-entry bimodal BHT + 4-entry RAS, 1-bit EX verify (no target compare)
motivation:
The champion (hyp-20260929-001-r1s0, 53.4 MHz, 449k cycles per CoreMark
iteration) has no prediction. next_pc is always pc+4. Every taken branch,
JAL and JALR redirects from EX, and the wrong-path IF/ID slot becomes a
bubble. IF and ID share one cycle, so each taken control-flow instruction
costs exactly 1 cycle. That is about 13% of dynamic instructions, or
about 8% of all cycles.

hyp-20260929-003-r1s2 measured this directly. A 64-entry BTB with 2-bit
counters and a RAS cut CoreMark cycles by 6.8% (4.49M to 4.18M) at flat
Fmax. That run was on the 5.4 MHz divider-bound core. LESSONS.md says to
re-apply it on the champion, where it becomes timing-relevant. There the
32-bit `actual_next != pred_next` compare sits after forwarding and the
branch compare, and drives redirect -> PC mux and flush_id. That is
nearly the same depth as the current critical path (regfile LUT-RAM ->
bypass -> fwd mux -> 32-bit adder -> dmem BSRAM address, 12 levels).

This core has one property a predictor can use. IF and ID are merged, so
the whole instruction word (io_imemData) is available in the fetch cycle.
In the timed FPGA netlist it even comes straight from a register (the
LFSR in core_bench_si.sv). A BTB therefore adds nothing: IF can decode
the opcode and compute the exact direct target (pc + B/J-imm) in the
same cycle. Only a direction bit is needed, from a tagless 2-bit counter
table, plus a return-address stack for `ret`. As a result:
  - direct targets are always right: no BTB tag, capacity or alias
    misses, and every JAL is predicted with no cold miss;
  - EX never compares 32-bit PCs for branches and JAL. A branch
    mispredicts iff `branch_cond XOR pred_taken`, which fits in the LUT
    that already forms `is_branch & branch_cond`. So redirect keeps
    today's depth;
  - a return is checked by an equality between the forwarded rs1 and the
    carried RAS target. That is the same depth as the existing BEQ
    comparator, with no adder in front of it.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a fetch-stage next-PC predictor and verify it in EX so that no
32-bit compare and no new adder land on the redirect path. Correctly
predicted taken branches, all JALs and correctly predicted returns cost
0 bubbles instead of 1. A mispredict costs 1 bubble, the same as a taken
branch costs today. Predictor state only affects performance: EX checks
every prediction, and exactly one wrong-path instruction can be in
flight (the IF slot), which the existing flush_id on redirect already
kills.

1. IF-side predecode (if_stage.sv, or a new rtl/branch_predictor.sv
   instantiated from core.sv). All of it is computed from raw imem_data
   and gated by imem_ready (no prediction on an imem-stall NOP):
     is_br   = opcode 1100011 and funct3 not in {2,3}
     is_jal  = opcode 1101111
     is_ret  = opcode 1100111, funct3 0, rd = x0, rs1 in {x1,x5},
               imm[11:0] = 0
     is_call = (JAL or JALR) with rd in {x1,x5}
     tgt     = pc + (is_jal ? J-imm : B-imm)   (one 32-bit adder)
   Never predict taken for a direct target with imm[1] = 1 (misaligned
   target). EX traps those without redirecting and the fall-through
   path is already correct.
     bht_ctr    = bht[pc[9:2]]   (256 x 2-bit, async-read LUT-RAM,
                                  no reset; `initial` loop -> 2'b01 so
                                  Verilator, Gowin and yosys agree)
     pred_taken = valid & !imm[1] & (is_jal | (is_br & bht_ctr[1]))
     ras_pred   = valid & is_ret & (ras_cnt != 0)
     pred_npc   = ras_pred ? ras_top : pred_taken ? tgt : pc + 4
   PC update: redirect ? redirect_target : (!stall ? pred_npc : pc).
   Redirect keeps priority over stall, as today. Keep redirect out of
   the IF NOP mux and the hazard compare, as in the champion.

2. Values carried in ID/EX (core_pkg.sv id_ex_t, plus the if_id_t
   bundle), zeroed by the existing reset/flush:
     pred_taken (1), ras_pred (1), bht_ctr (2),
     alt_target[31:0] = pred_taken ? pc+4 : tgt   (address used if the
                        direction guess is wrong)
     ras_tgt[31:2]    = ras_top                   (for the return check)
   ID/EX captures in exactly the cycles in which the PC takes pred_npc
   (stall_id is a subset of stall_if; an imem stall gives an invalid
   NOP). So the carried bits always match the prediction that steered
   fetch.

3. EX verification (ex_stage.sv). The redirect logic becomes:
     br_ok    = is_branch & !imm[1]            (register bits only)
     br_miss  = br_ok & (branch_cond ^ pred_taken)
     ret_hit  = ras_pred & (rs1_fwd[31:1] == {ras_tgt, 1'b0})
     jr_miss  = is_jalr & !ret_hit
     redirect = valid & (br_miss | jr_miss)   // JAL never redirects
     redirect_target = is_jalr ? (misalign ? pc+4 : {jalr_sum[31:1],0})
                               : alt_target
   A misaligned JALR that was ret-predicted redirects to pc+4. One that
   was not predicted also redirects to pc+4, which is harmless: an extra
   refetch of the correct address. The misaligned-branch and JAL trap
   semantics (no redirect, pc_next = pc+4, reg_write cleared) are
   unchanged. pc_next and all RVFI fields in EX/MEM are computed exactly
   as today. branch_target and the JAL pc+imm adder leave the redirect
   path because alt_target comes from a register.

4. BHT update, taken fully off EX timing. Write from the EX/MEM register
   (add bht_ctr and ctrl.is_branch to ex_mem_t; branch_taken already
   exists):
     if (ex_mem.valid & is_branch)
       bht[ex_mem.pc[9:2]] <= taken ? sat_inc(ctr) : sat_dec(ctr)
   The new value comes from the carried counter, not from a
   read-modify-write. So repeated writes while EX/MEM is held by a dmem
   stall are idempotent and need no gating. The one-cycle-late update
   only affects 1-2-instruction loops, and only for performance.

5. 4-entry RAS (circular pointer plus saturating count), updated in IF
   only when the IF instruction really advances:
     if_fire = imem_ready & !stall_if & !redirect
   Push pc+4 on is_call and pop on is_ret. The speculation window is one
   instruction deep: the IF instruction is on the wrong path iff EX
   redirects in that cycle. With this gating, the RAS only ever sees
   correct-path calls and returns and needs no repair. If Gowin reports
   redirect -> RAS clock-enable as critical, drop the !redirect term.
   Correctness is unaffected (EX still verifies); only RAS accuracy after
   mispredicts drops.

Expected effect: fewer cycles, at least matching r1s2's 6.8%. Every JAL
is predicted with no cold miss, direct targets are exact, returns are
covered, and a 256-entry tagless BHT aliases less than a 64-entry tagged
BTB. Estimate: 6-9% fewer cycles.
Fmax should stay about flat (53.4 MHz, within +/-3%):
  - the redirect cone keeps its depth: one XOR folded into the existing
    branch_cond AND-OR, and the target mux fed from registers;
  - the new IF paths (register -> imm -> 32-bit add -> 3:1 mux -> PC,
    and PC -> 256x2 LUT-RAM -> select) are about 10 ns against an 18.7
    ns period;
  - the BHT write port is driven only by EX/MEM registers.
Net: fitness +6-9% (118.9 -> about 127-129 iter/s), which clears the
4.6% acceptance bar. Area: about +150-250 LUT4, +~110 FF (ID/EX and
EX/MEM fields, RAS), 16 LUT-RAM16 blocks, no DSP or BSRAM.

Invariants: decoder, illegal and EBREAK discipline untouched. rvfi_order
and the retirement point unchanged. Wrong-path instructions never retire
(same single flush_id mechanism as today). Nothing in the predictor
touches memory, so memory bounds are unaffected.

title: Flatten both EX walls: ID-precomputed pc+imm/pc+4/imm results, one-hot ALU result mux, carry-chain branch compare, no-redirect misalign traps
motivation:
A Gowin timing run on the r2s1 champion (place option 0, 66.7 MHz, 14.97 ns
data path) shows two walls within 0.25 ns of each other. Both start at
the regfile BSRAM (2.26 ns clock-to-out) or rs?_data flop, then the 2-level
one-hot forwarding AND-OR:
(A) redirect cone, 20.295 ns arrival: fwd -> 29-cell compare carry chain
    (done at 12.7 ns) -> EIGHT LUT levels of redirect / misalign_fault /
    redirect_target / PC D-mux (u_if n328 -> n76 -> n71 -> n70_s7/s8/s2/s1) ->
    pc D. The EQ variant (paths 3, 5, 7-12, 10 levels) runs fwd -> a 4-level
    XOR-reduce tree -> redirect (fanout 20/35) -> pc CE. The same redirect
    also feeds flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl RESET (20.054 ns).
(B) ALU wall, 20.065 ns arrival: rs2_data flop -> fwd (2) -> alu_a AUIPC
    mux (1, fanout 12) -> shifter (2-3) -> SIX levels of alu_op-decoded
    result mux + is_jump link mux (n1391/n1375 chain) ->
    EX/MEM.alu_result.
Fixing only A leaves B at 20.07 ns, so both must be cut in the same change.
Everything proposed is cycle-identical (same 4,527,646 cycles), so the whole
Fmax gain shows up in the score.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move operand-independent work into ID and replace encoded muxes with
registered one-hot selects, so each EX cone is fwd -> one arithmetic block ->
1-2 LUTs -> flop.
1. ID precomputes two values and registers them in ID/EX. pc_imm = pc + imm
   is the B/J target and the AUIPC value. pc4 = pc + 4 is the JAL/JALR link
   and the misaligned-JALR target. ID also forms one registered imm_res =
   LUI ? imm : AUIPC ? pc_imm : pc4 (for JAL/JALR). EX no longer has the
   alu_a = is_auipc ? pc : rs1 mux (alu_a = rs1 always), no ALU_LUI arm, no
   in.pc + in.imm adder, and no separate is_jump ? pc_plus4 mux on
   alu_result.
2. ALU result as a flat AND-OR driven by registered one-hot group selects
   decoded in ID: sel_addsub, sel_logic, sel_slt, sel_sll, sel_sr, sel_imm
   (imm_res), sel_div. Plus the sub-op bits: sub, logic op[1:0], slt
   unsigned, sra. Logic is one LUT per bit: (a,b,op1,op0). The AND-OR over
   7 sources is 2 LUT levels, replacing about 6 levels of alu_op decode
   mux.
3. Operand b: give the ALU its own AND-OR that folds the immediate in as a
   5th one-hot source. ID zeroes the rs2 forwarding selects when alu_src=1.
   alu_b is then 2 levels instead of fwd (2) + alu_src mux (1). The plain
   forwarded rs2 (store data, compare, MUL, divider, RVFI) keeps the
   existing 4-source mux.
4. Branch compare on carry chains only. Take A = {a[31]^s, a[30:0]} and
   B = {b[31]^s, b[30:0]}, where s = ~funct3[1] flips the sign bit for
   signed compares. Compute lt_ab = A < B and lt_ba = B < A as two parallel
   chains (~1.5 ns each), which replaces the 4-level XOR-reduce EQ.
   cond = f3[2] ? (lt_ab ^ f3[0]) : ((lt_ab|lt_ba) ^ ~f3[0]), which is ONE
   LUT4.
5. Take the misalign traps off the redirect cone. A misaligned JAL (imm[1],
   known in ID) is decoded in ID as a trap: is_illegal=1, reg_write=0,
   is_jump=0. It never redirects, and it retires with pc_wdata=pc+4 as it
   does today. A taken misaligned branch no longer redirects, because pc+4
   is already being fetched. EX still sets is_illegal, and branches write no
   rd. ID registers br_ok = is_branch & !br_misalign. Then
   redirect = is_jump | (br_ok & cond), and
   redirect_target = is_jalr ? (agu[1] ? pc4 : {agu[31:1],0}) : pc_imm.
   branch_taken no longer touches target data. Only JALR's AGU sum and one
   early agu[1] select still do.
6. PC register in explicit D/CE form: CE = redirect | !stall_if,
   D = redirect ? redirect_target : pc+4.

title: Registered late redirect from EX/MEM plus fetch-time JAL/BTFN steering, taking the EX->PC cone off the critical path
motivation:
In the champion (hyp-20260929-002-r2s1: 67.9 MHz, 4.53M cycles), the worst
path runs from the regfile BSRAM (u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s) through u_ex into
u_if/pc_30: 40 cells and 20.3 ns arrival. On all three placement seeds it
is the same cone: BSRAM Tco -> one-hot fwd AND-OR -> 32-bit carry chain
(branch magnitude compare, or the rs1+imm AGU for the JALR target) ->
branch_taken / misalign_fault -> redirect -> redirect_target mux ->
pc-hold/pc+4 mux -> 32 PC flops. redirect also fans out to flush_id
(ID/EX valid and ctrl clear). r2s0 had a flop regfile and forwarding in
EX and hit the same wall (67.7 MHz, u_fwd > u_ex > u_if > u_id), so the
limit is the redirect cone itself, not the regfile technology. Every
earlier fix (AGU split, MUL pipelining, registered one-hot selects) left
this cone in place. It is the structural reason Fmax is stuck at ~68 MHz.

The ALU path (fwd -> adder/shifter -> result mux -> EX/MEM.alu_result)
and the AGU path (fwd -> rs1+imm -> dmem BSRAM address) share its prefix
but end in a flop or BSRAM address register. They avoid the redirect
decision, the two-level PC mux and its high fanout. Taking the redirect
decision out of the same cycle as the compare should buy about 2-4 LUT
levels plus the fanout, roughly 15-20% Fmax, before those paths take over.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Resolve control flow in EX as now, but register the result: the redirect
that steers fetch comes from the EX/MEM flops, one cycle later. Recover
the lost cycle by steering fetch from the raw instruction word in IF,
because IF and ID share a cycle and io_imemData is available there.

1. EX computes `mispredict` = valid & !kill & (is_jalr |
   (is_branch & !br_misalign & (branch_cond ^ pred_taken))). This is the
   same LUT depth as today's `branch_taken`. It is registered as
   EX/MEM.redirect. The redirect target is the existing registered
   EX/MEM.pc_next, which already holds the misalign-trap pc+4, the JALR
   target, the branch target or pc+4. EX no longer drives the PC.
2. `kill` = EX/MEM.redirect is a flop output. For one cycle it:
   a) loads pc <= EX/MEM.pc_next, taking priority over every stall;
   b) flushes ID/EX (valid plus side-effect ctrl, as today);
   c) makes EX/MEM capture a bubble ('0) for the wrong-path instruction
      now in EX;
   d) gates div_start / div_stall and the load/MUL-use stall for that
      instruction, so a wrong-path DIV or load cannot stall or start the
      divider.
   A branch or JALR in EX/MEM is never a memory op, so dmem_stall never
   holds EX/MEM while kill is high, and the redirect bit is high for
   exactly one cycle.
3. IF predecodes io_imemData (valid only when imem_ready):
   - JAL with an aligned target (instr[21]=0) is predicted taken.
   - A backward conditional branch (instr[31]=1, legal funct3, instr[8]=0)
     is predicted taken; all other branches are predicted not taken.
   One 32-bit adder computes pc + (J-imm or B-imm), selected by opcode.
   Then pc <= kill ? EX/MEM.pc_next : stall ? pc : (pred_taken ? tgt : pc+4).
   This path starts at the imem data flop (the LFSR in the timed bench),
   not after forwarding, so it is short. pred_taken travels in if_id_t and
   id_ex_t. JAL never redirects in EX. Misaligned JAL/branches are never
   predicted, trap in EX with pc_next = pc+4, and so need no redirect.

taken branch/JAL/JALR (about 13% of instructions): JAL goes 1 -> 0,
correctly predicted branches go 0 or 1 -> 0, mispredicted branches go
1 -> 2, and JALR goes 1 -> 2. With a 25-35% BTFN miss rate on CoreMark,
total cycles stay within about +/-3%. Fmax gains from removing
compare -> redirect -> PC-mux -> PC and redirect -> flush_id from the
fwd/carry-chain cone. The expected next wall is the EX ALU ->
EX/MEM.alu_result path, about 2-4 LUT levels shorter, so we estimate
about 80 MHz: +15% Fmax at roughly flat IPC.

This is orthogonal to r2s2's BHT+RAS predictor, which can later replace
the BTFN rule (tagless BHT bit) and send `ret` to a RAS target. The
EX-side check stays 1-bit, with no 32-bit PC compare anywhere.

title: Re-apply r2s2 fetch-time predecode predictor (256x2 BHT + exact pc+imm target + 4-entry RAS) on the r2s1 champion with a depth-neutral EX redirect
motivation:
Every taken branch or jump on the champion (r2s1, 67.9 MHz, 4.53M
cycles) costs one bubble, because IF and ID share a cycle and redirect
comes from EX. r2s2 removed almost all of those bubbles on the older
r1s0 base (-7.0% cycles, 4.49M -> 4.18M) at flat Fmax. LESSONS says to
re-apply it on the r2s1 champion.
A fresh Gowin timing run of the champion shows why it has to be
depth-neutral. The top 25 paths are
regfile -> EX fwd -> compare/JALR adder -> redirect -> u_if/pc (20.30 ns)
and redirect -> ID/EX flush (20.05 ns). There are also ALU paths
rs2 -> fwd -> alu_a -> ALU -> alu_result at 20.07 ns.
Because the ALU path is equally long, registering the redirect would
gain only about 1% Fmax while doubling the mispredict penalty. So the
win is IPC at unchanged Fmax, and nothing may be added after the
forwarded-operand compare on the redirect cone.

instruction word:
- JAL: predict taken to pc + J-imm (exact target, so EX never
  redirects a JAL). If J-imm[1]=1, predict pc+4 so the misaligned-target
  trap still continues at pc+4 as today.
- BRANCH: pred_taken = bht[pc[9:2]][1] && !B-imm[1], with target pc + B-imm.
  One shared adder pc + (jal ? J-imm : B-imm) on flop-sourced inputs.
- RET (JALR, rd=x0, rs1 in {x1,x5}, imm=0): predict the top of a
  4-entry RAS. CALL (JAL/JALR with rd in {x1,x5}): push pc+4. Update
  the RAS only when the instruction is really accepted into ID/EX
  (valid && !stall_if && !redirect).
- next_pc = redirect ? redirect_target
          : pred_jal_or_br_taken ? pc+imm : pred_ret ? ras_top : pc+4.
  redirect must stay the last-level select; the prediction mux sits
  before it, driven only by flops (pc, imem word, BHT, RAS).
- The BHT is 256 x 2-bit (LUT-RAM or flops, no reset needed for
  correctness). The read counter travels down the pipe. The update is
  written at MEM from registered EX/MEM fields (pc, is_branch,
  branch_taken, carried counter), so no EX combinational logic feeds
  the BHT.
ID/EX carries: pred_taken, pred_ret, pred_target (RAS value, 32b), and
alt_target = pred_taken ? pc+4 : pc+B-imm, computed in IF/ID from
values that already exist there.

- branch: redirect_br = is_branch && (pred_taken ? !branch_cond
                                                : (branch_cond && !br_misalign)).

  branch_taken LUT level.

                                 && !misalign).
  This equality compare is no deeper than the existing BEQ compare.

  redirect_target = is_jalr ? (misalign ? pc+4 : {jalr_sum[31:1],0})
                            : alt_target.
  For branches this target is now a registered value, which also
  removes the in.pc+in.imm adder from the redirect_target cone.
- EX/MEM.pc_next stays the true next PC, so RVFI and formal are
  unchanged. The misaligned JAL/branch trap semantics are unchanged.

non-ret JALRs and BHT aliasing are the residual) at flat Fmax, possibly
slightly better since branch_target leaves the redirect_target mux.

title: Regfile out of BSRAM into LUT-RAM (drop 2.26 ns BSRAM tC2Q) plus cut the tied fwd2b->adder ALU wall
motivation:
I re-ran `make timing` on the r3s0 champion (82.6 MHz on place_option 0).
Four of the top five paths start at the regfile BSRAM
cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s: branch -> redirect -> ID/EX valid flush
(17.394 ns), redirect -> PC (17.374), MUL (17.358) and ALU (17.348).
Gowin infers the 32x32 regfile as SDPB BSRAM by absorbing the read
address, so EX operand source [0] is the BSRAM's DO pin. The per-cell
report for path 1 shows BSRAM tC2Q = 2.260 ns, then a 1.376 ns route
from the BSRAM column to the first forwarding LUT. A fabric DFF has
about 0.4 ns tC2Q and can sit next to the EX logic. After that come
only two forwarding LUT levels, a 5-LUT branch/redirect cone
(pc_ce_s25..s2, fanout 35), then the flush LUT.
Path 3 (17.374 ns, 27 cells) is tied: it starts at the fabric flop

title: Pre-resolved EX operands: forwarding moved to the ID->ID/EX edge, async-read regfile, every EX path starts at a flop
motivation:
`make timing TARGET=bench` on the r3s0 champion (p0: 82.6 MHz) shows the
top 8 path groups within 0.09 ns of each other (17.31-17.39 ns arrival,
about 12.05 ns data path). Every one of them starts at the same prefix,
the BSRAM regfile output feeding the EX forwarding AND-OR:
  redirect -> ID/EX.valid reset / PC, regfile -> DSP -> EX/MEM.mul_prod,
  fwd2b flop -> alu_b mux -> adder -> EX/MEM.alu_result,
  regfile -> fwd -> ALU, regfile -> ID/EX mem_read/mem_write/br_ok flush.

the mux, so the shared BSRAM + forwarding prefix is now the whole
remaining wall. Cutting it moves all the near-tied walls at once, which
is what the r3s0 lesson asks for.

Resolve forwarding one cycle early. Each ID/EX operand register then holds
the final architectural operand, and every EX path starts at a plain
fabric flop (tC2Q ~0.23 ns) with no mux in front.

   within budget). It has 2 combinational read ports and is read in ID
   from the raw imem rs1/rs2 fields. The write lands at the clock edge and
   is visible to the next cycle's read, so wb_q and the fwd [3] source
   are deleted. It must NOT map to BSRAM: a BSRAM would put tC2Q back.

   cycle's writers. They are no longer registered. They drive a
   next-operand mux in front of ID/EX:
     E = EX-stage alu_result (producer = ID/EX; loads/MULs interlocked as
         today, so E is only ever an ALU/imm_res/div result)
     M = MEM-stage write-back value (mem_stage `result`: load data / MUL
         half / EX/MEM.alu_result; enabled by reg_write_eff)
     W = MEM/WB.result (the regfile write happening this cycle, w_en)

title: Depth-neutral fetch predictor on r3s0: predecode JAL/BHT branch/RAS ret, ret verified on the existing BEQ carry chains
motivation:
The r3s0 champion (85.544 MHz, 4,527,646 cycles) has no prediction. Its
worst path is BSRAM regfile -> EX forward mux -> two sign-adjusted `<`
carry chains -> branch_cond LUT -> redirect LUT -> flush_id / PC D-mux
(17.39 ns, 9 cells). IF and ID share a cycle and redirect comes from EX,
so every taken branch, JAL and JALR costs one bubble.
The fetch-predecode predictor has been measured twice on older bases:
r2s2 cut cycles 7.7% (4.49M -> 4.18M) and r3s2 cut them 6.9%
(4.53M -> 4.21M). The design is a 256x2 tagless BHT, an exact pc+B/J-imm
target computed from the raw imem word, and a RAS. LESSONS.md
(r3s0, r3s1, r3s2) says to stack it on r3s0 and keep it off the
now-shallow redirect -> PC D/CE cone. The one piece of r2s2/r3s2 that
did add depth to that cone was the return check: a separate 31-bit
XOR-reduce equality between forwarded rs1 and the RAS target, ORed into
redirect. r3s2's critical path was exactly regfile -> u_ex -> u_if/pc
(19.1 ns, 12 levels). On r3s0 that cone is the entire Fmax wall, so the
predictor must add zero LUT levels to it.
In the timed netlist io_imemData comes straight from a flop (the LFSR in
fpga/core_bench_si.sv). The fetch-side adder, BHT and RAS paths
therefore start at flops and stay well under the period.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a fetch-time next-PC predictor whose EX verification reuses the
existing redirect logic without adding a single LUT level:

1. Fetch predecode (if_stage.sv plus new rtl/branch_predictor.sv). It
   works on the post-flush imem word, is gated by valid, and must match
   the decoder's legality exactly:
     is_br   = opcode 1100011 and funct3 not in {2,3}
     is_jal  = opcode 1101111
     is_ret  = opcode 1100111, funct3=0, rd=x0, rs1 in {x1,x5}, imm[11:0]=0
     is_call = (JAL, or JALR with funct3=0) with rd in {x1,x5}
     tgt     = pc + (instr[3] ? J-imm : B-imm)   (one adder, flop inputs)
     pred_tk = valid & !imm[1] & (is_jal | is_br & bht[pc[9:2]][1])
     pred_rt = valid & is_ret                    (always use RAS top)
     pred_npc = pred_rt ? ras_top : pred_tk ? tgt : pc+4
   PC: pc_ce = redirect | !stall (unchanged); pc_d = redirect ?
   redirect_target : pred_npc. Redirect stays the last 2:1 select, and
   everything before it is driven by flops. A misaligned JAL or branch
   target (imm[1]=1) is never predicted, so the ID-decoded trap
   semantics are unchanged (no redirect, continue at pc+4).
   The BHT has 256 x 2-bit entries in async-read LUT-RAM, no reset, and
   an `initial` weakly-not-taken value. The RAS is a 4-entry
   *shift-register* stack (push shifts down, pop shifts up), so ras_top
   is a flop with no read mux. It updates only when the IF instruction
   really advances: fire = valid & !stall_if & !redirect. Because the
   one wrong-path slot is excluded, no repair is needed.

2. New registered ID/EX fields, computed in ID from the IF payload and
   values ID already has:
     alt_tgt[31:0] = pred_tk ? pc4 : pc_imm     (address if direction wrong)
     ret_tgt[31:0] = pred_rt ? ras_top : 32'b0  (exactly 0 unless ret-predicted)
     chk           = br_ok | pred_rt            (cleared on flush like br_ok)
     pred          = pred_tk | pred_rt
     jr_redir      = is_jalr & !pred_rt         (cleared on flush)
     bht_ctr[1:0]
   These fields hold on stall, like the other data fields.

3. EX verification (ex_stage.sv) uses the same single redirect LUT4:
     redirect = jr_redir | (chk & (branch_cond ^ pred))
   This has four inputs: three flops plus the existing cond LUT. JAL is
   always predicted at fetch and never redirects. A ret-predicted JALR
   has branch_op = 000 (BEQ, the decoder default), so branch_cond is
   rs1 == cmp_b and redirect fires iff rs1 != ret_tgt. That compare runs
   on the existing lt_ab/lt_ba carry chains with
     cmp_b_src = rs2 | in.ret_tgt
   It is a separate operand used only by the comparator, and it adds one
   OR input to the rs2 AND-OR's last LUT. For a ret, rs2 is x0 (imm=0),
   so fwd2 = 0000 and rs2 = 0. For every other instruction ret_tgt = 0.

title: One-level EX operand muxes: wb_q moved to an ID write-first bypass, 2-bit encoded forwarding selects (LUT4+MUX2_LUT5)
motivation:
The r4s0 champion (94.3 MHz) runs the critical path
u_id/g_lane[0].fwd1_q -> EX forwarding AND-OR -> compare chains ->
redirect -> ID/EX flush (15.846 ns arrival, 10 cells). Every EX wall
(branch/redirect, adder -> alu_result, AGU, MUL DSP input) starts with
the same operand mux: a one-hot AND-OR over 4 register sources
(rs_val, EX/MEM.alu_result, MEM/WB.result, wb_q), plus the immediate
for alu_b/add_b. A 4-source one-hot AND-OR is an 8-input function (10 for
alu_b), which cannot fit one Gowin LUT4. It maps to 2 LUT levels with a
general route between them. An encoded 4:1 mux (2 select + 4 data =
6 inputs) maps to Gowin's native two LUT4 + MUX2_LUT5 inside one CLS, so
it costs one LUT level plus a ~0.2 ns in-slice mux. The timed harness
(fpga/core_bench_si.sv) drives io_imemData from an LFSR flop, so ID-stage
paths start at a fabric DFF and have slack to spare. The r4s1 lesson
assumed a BSRAM imem start, but that does not hold in the timed netlist.

title: Registered EX/MEM redirect + fetch-time JAL/BTFN steering on the r4s0 champion
motivation:
The r4s0 champion (94.3 MHz) is walled by one cone: g_lane fwd1_q -> EX
operand AND-OR -> sign-adjusted compare chains -> branch_cond -> redirect
-> flush_id / pc_ce / pc_d -> ID/EX side-effect ctrl flops and the 32 PC
flops (10 cells, 15.85 ns arrival). r4s0 already cut the ALU/adder wall, so
the redirect -> flush/PC fanout (3+ LUTs plus two high-fanout routes after
the compare) is the only thing between the forwarding mux and the clock
edge. r3s1 showed that registering the redirect and steering fetch with
predecoded JAL/BTFN cuts cycles by 2.4% (4.42M vs 4.53M, same cycle model
as r4s0), and that the resulting gain was mostly Fmax.

EX computes mispredict = is_jalr | (is_branch & br_ok & (branch_cond ^
pred_taken)) and the correct next PC (pc_imm / pc4 / JALR agu), and

title: Zero-depth fetch predictor on r4s0: BHT+JAL predecode, EX verify by funct3[0] flip, RAS checked on the existing compare chains
motivation:
The r4s0 champion (94.3 MHz, 4.527M cycles) is fully balanced. A fresh Gowin
timing run of it (place option 0) puts the top 25 setup paths within
0.2 ns of each other (10.35-10.52 ns data delay): fwd1_q -> branch compare
-> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl RESET (15.846), MEM/WB.result -> fwd
-> ALU -> EX/MEM.alu_result (15.843), fwd -> DSP -> mul_prod (15.82),
redirect -> pc CE/D (15.79) and fwd -> agu/misalign -> EX/MEM.ctrl.reg_write
(15.78). Cutting any one of these walls (e.g. a late/registered redirect as
in r3s1) buys ~0 Fmax. The remaining lever is cycles: every taken
branch/JAL/ret still costs one bubble because IF and ID share a cycle and the
redirect happens in EX. The BHT+JAL+RAS predictor cut cycles to 4214733
(-6.9%) on both r3s2 and r4s2, which is +7.4% fitness at flat Fmax. r4s2
lost that gain because Fmax fell to 79 MHz. Its lesson blames the RAS check
(`cmp_b = rs2 | ret_tgt`, an extra OR after the post-forward rs2 mux) plus
unrouted extra logic. This hypothesis re-applies the predictor with a strict
rule: after the forwarding muxes, the redirect cone keeps exactly the same
LUT structure (compare chains -> 1 cond LUT -> 1 redirect LUT), and every
new signal on it is a registered ID/EX field.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a fetch-time predictor whose EX verification is a pure re-encoding of
the existing redirect logic, so cycles fall ~6-7% with no added depth on the
tied 10.5 ns cluster.

IF (same cycle as ID, reads raw io_imemData):
 * Predecode: is_br (opcode 1100011), is_jal (1101111), is_ret (JALR, rd=x0,
   rs1=x1/x5, imm=0), is_call (JAL/JALR with rd=x1/x5).
 * BHT: 256 x 2-bit counters in LUT-RAM (distributed_ram, init weakly-not-
   taken), async read at pc[9:2] (pc is a fabric flop, so the read is early).
 * pred = (is_jal & !instr[21]) | (is_br & bht[1] & !instr[8]) | (is_ret &
   ras_valid). Misaligned B/J targets are never predicted, so they still
   trap without redirecting, exactly as today.
 * pred_tgt = is_ret ? ras_top : pc + imm_bj, where imm_bj is one LUT3/bit
   (instr[3] selects the J- vs the B-immediate) feeding its own 32-bit adder,
   so it does not go through imm_gen's opcode case.
 * pc_d = redirect ? redirect_target : (pred ? pred_tgt : pc+4). Keep
   redirect as the LAST mux level: the sequential/predicted value is
   resolved before redirect arrives, so each pc bit stays one LUT
   (MUX2_LUT5 at worst). pc_ce is unchanged (redirect | !stall_if).

   deliberately leaves out redirect/flush_id, so RAS CE is not on the EX

   for next_pc/RVFI and ctrl_with_trap.

   AND-OR is the same 2 LUT levels as a 4-term one (alu_b is already 5-term
   on the tied ALU path).

   chains.

title: Flatten the whole tied wall set on r5s1: encoded 3-source EX muxes + DSP-absorbable mul_prod + divider/ID/IF level cuts
motivation:
A `make timing` run on the r5s1 champion (place_option 0: 97.4 MHz,
6-level worst path) shows a flat wall. Paths 1-19 all sit within 0.17 ns
(15.562 -> 15.393 ns arrival), spread over five independent groups:
  (a) EX operand mux -> DSP -> reg_q.mul_prod (15.562, 6 cells; EX/MEM.alu_result_31 source)
  (b) EX operand mux (fwd1_q / fwd2b_q / MEM/WB.result) -> adder/shifter -> alu_result (15.55)
      and -> compare -> redir_q / ctrl.reg_write (15.52 / 15.51)
  (c) divider internals: b_q -> negate -> dvsr_q (15.496), rem_q_sel -> fix-up
      negate -> result_q (15.472), a_q -> quo_q (15.465)
  (d) ID: lfsr (imem) / imem_ready -> NOP-substitution mux -> decoder alu_op
      -> asel.sub -> imm_sub / imm_res (15.44 / 15.33)
  (e) IF: pc -> pc+imm_f carry chain -> 3-way pc_d mux -> pc (15.415)
r5s0 showed that the EX-only change (wb_q moved into an ID write-first bypass,
plus encoded 3-source muxes) is worth about 1 LUT + route on the r4s0 base.
Applied alone here it would be capped within ~0.15 ns by (c)/(d)/(e), which
is the r3s1/r5s1 lesson: cutting one of several tied walls buys nothing.
So cut all five groups in one cycle-identical change (the divider latency
grows by 2 cycles, and CoreMark's timed loop runs almost no DIV/REM).

title: Decoupled front end: 2-entry fetch queue that keeps fetching through backend stalls (PC CE off the hazard cone) + registered-operand 2-cycle MUL hidden by it
motivation:
The r5s1 champion (101.5 MHz, 4.42M cycles, ~2.26 CoreMark/MHz) runs
under a ~22% random imem-stall stream: (state & 0x7F) < 100 draws once
per cycle, independent of whether the core requests anything. At the
ideal CPI of 1.0 this alone is 1/0.78 = 1.28 CPI, the single largest
cycle component. Every earlier round attacked branch bubbles or EX
depth. None touched the fetch/backend coupling, and nothing in log.jsonl
tried a fetch queue or prefetch.

Today IF and ID share a cycle, and the IF/ID payload is combinational.
So on every backend stall cycle (load-use bubble, MUL-use bubble, dmem
stall on ~30% of instructions at 0.28 extra cycles each, divide), the
PC holds and the word imem delivered that cycle is thrown away. The
same PC is then refetched and faces the 22% stall draw again. Imem
stalls and backend stalls therefore serialize. Rough budget over the
10 iterations:
  - dmem stalls: ~210k cycles
  - load-use: ~150k cycles
  - MUL-use: ~36k cycles (r2s0 minus r1s0)
That is ~400k backend-stall cycles. In each of them imem is ready 78%
of the time, and a banked word later replaces an imem-stall cycle
unless a redirect flushes it first. Redirects are rare within the ~4.5
cycle mean gap to the next imem stall, so roughly 0.78 x 0.83 of the
banked words pay off. That is about 250k cycles, or -5% to -6%.

Separately, the champion's worst path is EX/MEM.alu_result -> forward
mux -> 33x33 DSP -> EX/MEM.mul_prod (6 cells, 9.85 ns). It sits in the
near-tied EX cluster that the r4s0 report showed within 0.2 ns. The
decoupled front end makes a 1-cycle EX occupancy bubble much cheaper,
because fetch banks a word during it. That lets the DSP take registered
operands and leave the forward mux entirely.

Two coupled structural changes. Both keep every EX/redirect cone at its
current depth or shallower.

(1) 2-entry fetch queue with same-cycle bypass (if_stage.sv, hazard_unit.sv, core.sv).
  - Queue entries e0 (head) and e1 hold {instr, pc, pred_taken}.
    cnt_q is in {0,1,2}; qv_q = (cnt_q != 0) and full_q = (cnt_q == 2)
    are plain registered flops. Add syn_keep replicas of qv_q, one per
    byte lane / per consumer group, so the ID input mux select never
    fans out more than ~8-16 loads.
  - ID input (the if_id_t bundle):
      instr = qv ? e0.instr : (imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP)
      pc    = qv ? e0.pc    : pc
      valid = qv | imem_ready
      pred  = qv ? e0.pred  : is_bwd_br_f

    hazard unit's if_id_rs1/rs2 become the same head-selected raw fields

    harmless as today.

      cnt=1: ID reads e0.

             pop & !fetched -> cnt=0

      cnt=2: no fetch. On pop, e0 <= e1 (cnt=1).

    flush_id exactly as today.

  - flush_if (the NOP mux) now keys on !qv & !imem_ready.
  - stall_if is kept only as the name for the ID-hold condition, or
    removed.

    reset, so Gowin absorbs them into the DSP A/B input registers:
      mul_a_q <= {rs1[31] & mul_sa, rs1}
      mul_b_q <= {rs2[31] & mul_sb, rs2}

    so the path is DSP input reg -> DSP -> output reg with no fabric LUT.
  - A phase flop mul_ph_q holds the handshake:

title: 256x2 BHT direction + 4-entry RAS on r5s1's registered-redirect fetch steering (verify feeds only redir_q)
motivation:
The r5s1 champion (101.5 MHz, 4.420M cycles) steers fetch with JAL
predecode and static BTFN, and registers the EX mispredict in redir_q.
That doubled the cost of every miss to 2 bubbles: every JALR (all
CoreMark returns plus the list-sort indirect calls) always redirects,
and every BTFN miss (forward-taken branches, loop exits) costs 2 cycles.
The BHT+JAL+RAS predictor measured 4.215M cycles (r3s2/r4s2/r5s2) at a
1-bubble penalty, 4.6% fewer than r5s1, even though every returning
JALR paid 2 bubbles in r5s1. The three earlier same-cycle-redirect
attempts lost about 1 ns because their verify and target logic sat on
the fwd -> compare -> redirect -> PC wall. LESSONS r5s2 says to retry on
r5s1, where that cone ends at a single flop. r5s1's critical path is
now fwd -> DSP -> mul_prod (15.56 ns, 6 cells), and IF paths start at
fabric flops (the LFSR imem word, pc, redir_q/redir_tgt_q), so IF has
slack for one more pc_d mux input and a small LUT-RAM read.

Measured with the reference ISS on the timed CoreMark window (2.922M
instructions): 49.4K JAL, 13.7K JALR (all returns, and a 4-entry RAS
hits 13.72K of them), 530K conditional branches (294K taken). BTFN misses
111K of them. The model cycles = 4.170M + 2*(JALR + branch misses)
reproduces r5s1's measured 4.4196M exactly (4.420M), and the no-predictor
4.528M (4.170M + J + R + Bt). A 256-entry bimodal agree-with-BTFN BHT
misses 39.6K branches (128 entries: 44.7K; 1024 entries: 39.5K; a
1024-entry gshare with 10 history bits: 33.4K, but it needs a
speculative GHR and a 64:1 LUT-RAM read at IF, which is not worth it).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep r5s1's pipeline, registered redirect, kill logic and JAL steering.
Replace BTFN with a trained direction predictor, and predict returns.

1. BHT (if_stage): 256 x 2-bit tagless counters in LUT-RAM
   (syn_ramstyle distributed_ram, `initial` zero), read asynchronously
   from the pc flop with index pc[9:2]. The counter stores "disagree
   with BTFN", so pred_dir = ctr[1] ^ imem[31] and the all-zero initial
   state behaves exactly like today's BTFN. This XOR folds into the
   existing pred_f LUT. pred_taken = valid_branch & aligned & pred_dir,
   and the 2-bit counter rides IF/ID -> ID/EX -> EX/MEM with the branch.
   Update is written from EX/MEM registered fields (all-flop write port,
   off every compare cone): we = EX/MEM valid & is_branch & !br_misalign,
   wdata = sat(ctr +/- (branch_taken ^ btfn_bit)), waddr = EX/MEM
   pc[9:2]. A repeated write while EX/MEM holds on a dmem stall is
   idempotent.

2. RAS (if_stage): 4-entry shift-register stack of flops. Predecode on
   the raw imem word, updated only when fetch accepts the instruction
   (pc_ce & !redir_q):
     push pc+4 on JAL/JALR with rd in {x1,x5}
     pop on JALR with rs1 in {x1,x5}, rd = x0, imm = 0, and pc_d = ras_top
   pc_d becomes a 4:1 (redir_tgt_q / ras_top / pc_imm_f / pc+4) with
   early selects, i.e. one LUT4 + MUX2_LUT5 slice. A wrong-path
   push/pop (at most one instruction per mispredict) is simply
   tolerated because every prediction is verified.

3. Verify (id_stage / ex_stage): a RAS-predicted JALR carries its
   target in the otherwise unused ID/EX pc_imm field (JALR's EX never
   reads pc_imm) plus a ras_pred bit. EX computes
     mispredict = (is_jalr & !(ras_pred & rs1[31:1] == pc_imm[31:1]))
                | (br_ok & mis_br)
   With imm = 0, the target is rs1 & ~1, so this is exact. A misaligned
   rs1 (bit 1 set) fails the compare and redirects to pc4 through the
   existing alt_tgt/misalign path. The equality tree is fwd mux ->
   3 LUT levels -> the mispredict LUT, and it feeds only redir_q,
   far from the 15.56 ns mul wall. redir_tgt_q, the kill, the
   div_start gating, pc_next and RVFI are all unchanged. mis_inv and
   alt_tgt keep their meaning, with pred_taken now from the BHT.

Expected: returns that are correctly predicted go from 2 bubbles to 0,
and BHT removes most of BTFN's forward-taken and loop-exit misses, each
of which was 2 bubbles. The target is fewer than r3s2's 4.215M cycles,
because JALs stay exact and most JALRs no longer redirect, so about
-5% to -6% cycles versus 4.420M at ~101 MHz (the IF-side additions sit
in slack and the EX verify ends at one flop). The gain is roughly
+5-7% fitness.
